messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Film Director
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Distraction: I distract myself with something else
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas is a 52-year-old American film director of European background who came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly estranged from himself in the aftermath of a life-threatening accident. He had been on location for a night shoot when the accident happened, working late with a small crew on a rural road closed for filming. A vehicle movement had to be reset, lights were being repositioned, and in the confusion of shouted cues, engine noise, and people moving through patches of darkness, Thomas found himself suddenly in the wrong place at the wrong time. He has never found a satisfying way to tell the story from beginning to end. When he tries, the account breaks apart. What comes instead are sharply defined images: the brutal white spill of production lights against black surroundings, a vehicle where it should not have been, the instant of realizing it was coming toward him, the flash of metal, the ground rushing up. He says the memory is “all pictures,” as if the event exists in frozen frames rather than words, and those frames remain painfully clear.

In the weeks afterward, Thomas was disturbed by how immediate those images felt. He did not describe a vague recollection but scenes with the kind of detail he would normally notice professionally: angles, contrast, glare, movement. That precision frightened him. He could not make the event cohere into a narrative he could master, and this left him circling around it mentally, asking why it had happened to him at all. He found himself returning to that question when he was alone in the morning, in the car, or after work when the house had gone quiet. There was no answer that settled him. Instead, the repeated searching seemed to leave him more aware of how abruptly life had split into before and after.

Since the accident, darkness has become especially hard for him to tolerate. On sets, he now avoids being present for night work when he can delegate it, and if he cannot, he stays close to banks of light or finds reasons to step away while scenes are being prepared. The combination of darkness and sudden sound is particularly potent. A dropped piece of equipment, a slammed production van door, an unexpected call over a speaker can make his whole body jolt before he has time to think. Crew members have noticed him whip around at noises that would once have been routine for him. He scans constantly now, listening for what might happen next, noticing every shift in sound on set and in ordinary life. Even at home, a pan clattering in the kitchen or a neighbor’s car backfiring can make him jump hard enough to spill a drink or lose his place in conversation.

Thomas has tried to manage this in ways that make sense to him. He keeps himself busy, filling the day with edits, scheduling decisions, emails, and streaming something in the background when he is not working, anything to prevent his mind from settling where the images can return. When a location scout proposes a dim warehouse, a tunnel, or an exterior night sequence, he often reshapes the plan or sends someone else. He tells himself this is practical, but he is also aware that he is arranging his life around not being in circumstances that remind him of the accident. Over time this has narrowed both his work and his relationship. His partner has watched him stay up later with television on, then hesitate to walk through a dark hallway without switching on multiple lights. Thomas feels exposed by this, ashamed not only of the reactions themselves but of what he thinks they say about him.

What weighs on him most is not only fear but the judgment he has come to make about himself. He had always thought of himself as composed under pressure, someone other people relied on when conditions were chaotic. Now he sees himself startling at ordinary sounds, avoiding darkness, and failing to say plainly what happened, and he has come to believe this means he is inadequate. He says his reactions show he is “a lousy coper.” More than once he has told his therapist that he scarcely recognizes himself. The person he knew—a director able to work through noise, unpredictability, and long nights—feels far away from the man who is now constantly on guard.

He finally sought help after a recent night shoot when a metal stand crashed to the ground behind him. He spun around so violently that the set went silent, and for a moment he could not speak. Later, sitting in his car and staring at his own reflection in the dark windshield, he felt the familiar thought with unusual force: I am not myself anymore. He has come to treatment because he does not want his life to keep shrinking around these moments, and because what frightens him most is the possibility that this unrecognizable version of himself is permanent.
